ch14_ex12_q1a: Party trick: in radian mode, type any number and press $\cos$ over and over; the display settles on $0.739\ldots$, the solution of $\cos x = x$.
Why only one solution: $x - \cos x$ has derivative $1 + \sin x \ge 0$, so it is increasing and can cross zero only once.
ch14_ex12_q1b: Estimate first: at $x = \frac{\pi}{6} \approx 0.524$, $\sin x = 0.5$ while $1 - x \approx 0.476$, so the root is just below $0.524$, matching $0.51$.
Uniqueness: $\sin x + x - 1$ has derivative $\cos x + 1 \ge 0$, so it is increasing and has only one zero.
ch14_ex12_q1c: Since $\cos x \le 1$, any solution needs $x^2 \le 1$, so a window of $-1.5 \le x \le 1.5$ is enough to see every intersection.
Check: $\cos(0.82) \approx 0.68$ and $0.82^2 \approx 0.67$, close enough at two decimal places.
ch14_ex12_q1d: Why no negative solutions: for $-\pi < x < 0$, $\sin x < 0 < x^2$; for $x \le -\pi$, $x^2 > 1 \ge \sin x$.
Similarly $x > 1$ gives $x^2 > 1$, so the non-zero solution must lie in $(0, 1)$; check $\sin(0.88) \approx 0.77 \approx 0.88^2$.
ch14_ex12_q2a: Spot the surd: $2.4 \approx 1 + \sqrt{2}$, a hint that $\frac{3\pi}{4}$-type angles are involved; indeed $2\sin\frac{3\pi}{4} + 1 = \sqrt{2} + 1$.
With $b = 1$ and $a = 2$, the value $-1$ at $\theta = \frac{\pi}{2}$ is the minimum, so $\sin\frac{n\pi}{2} = -1$; the smallest positive choice is $n = 3$.
ch14_ex12_q2b: The equal values at $0.4$ and $0.6$ put the maximum at $\theta = 0.5$, so half a period is $1$, the period is $2$, and $n = \frac{2\pi}{2} = \pi$.
ch14_ex12_q2c: The data dips to almost 0 but starts at 5, suggesting centre 5 and amplitude 5; the rule $5(1 - \sin 3\theta)$ can never go negative, which fits.
The minimum of $5 - 5\sin 3\theta$ is at $\theta = \frac{\pi}{6} \approx 0.52$, neatly between the two smallest data values at $0.4$ and $0.6$.
